opus-5.5.text:
So when I say research taste, I basically mean the bundle of intuitions that guide all the decisions you make in research that you can't easily justify from first principles. Research is full of these judgment calls: which problem do I work on? Is this idea promising or a dead end? This experiment gave a weird result. Is that a bug, noise, or something genuinely interesting? Should I keep pushing on this direction or cut my losses and pivot? How do I know when I've actually shown something versus fooling myself?

You can't really answer those by sitting down and reasoning everything out explicitly, because there's way too much uncertainty and too many options. So what good researchers have is a kind of trained gut sense, a learned model of how research tends to go, that lets them make those calls well and quickly.

I find it useful to break it into a few pieces. There's taste in choosing problems: having a sense of what's important, what's tractable, and what's going to teach you something even if it fails. There's taste in execution: knowing which experiment to run next, what the quick and dirty version looks like, when to be rigorous and when to just get signal. And there's taste in interpretation: looking at results and having good instincts for what they actually mean, being appropriately skeptical, noticing when something smells off.

The thing about research taste is that it's mostly learned through feedback loops, and in research those loops are really slow. You might work on a project for months before finding out whether your initial instinct was any good. So you only get a handful of data points a year, which is a big part of why it's so hard to develop, and why I think mentorship is so valuable. A mentor has already accumulated a lot of those data points and can short-circuit some of that process for you. When I'm mentoring people, a lot of what I'm trying to do is make my own intuitions legible: not just saying "do this," but explaining why I think it, so they can start building that model themselves.

r001.rationale: Defines research taste as a trained set of intuitions guiding research decisions, including which problems to pursue and whether to continue or pivot.

r002.rationale: Includes experimental design in research taste, describing instincts about which experiment to run next and how to get useful signal.

fable-5.1.text:
Research taste is kind of this fuzzy, catch-all term that people use to describe the intuitions that let an experienced researcher make good decisions in situations where there isn't a clear rule to follow. Things like: which problem is actually worth working on, which of the five experiments you could run next is going to be the most informative, when a result is interesting versus when it's an artifact you should be suspicious of, when to keep pushing on something and when to cut your losses and move on.

The way I think about it, it's basically a big collection of learned heuristics and pattern-matching that you accumulate from doing a lot of research and seeing what works and what doesn't. It's not one skill, it's a bundle. There's problem selection, there's experimental design, there's the skepticism and sanity-checking side, there's knowing how to communicate a result so people actually care. And people can be strong on some of these and weak on others.

I think the reason it gets talked about as this mysterious, almost mystical thing is that a lot of it is tacit. The senior researcher often can't fully articulate why they think an idea is bad, they just have a feeling, and the feeling tends to be right more often than chance. But I don't think it's actually magic. It's more like how a chess grandmaster looks at a board and immediately sees the few moves worth considering. They've just seen a lot of boards. The good news is that means it's learnable, and I think a lot of what mentorship is about is compressing that learning process by having someone with taste point out when your intuitions are off before you spend three months finding out the hard way.

r001.rationale: Defines research taste as intuitions that help experienced researchers make good decisions without clear rules, including which problem to pursue.

r002.rationale: Explicitly includes experimental design as part of research taste and gives choosing the next informative experiment as an example.

astra-6.text:
By research taste, I mean the ability to judge which research questions are worth working on and which approaches are likely to get you somewhere. There are lots of things you could investigate, and most of them won’t lead to a particularly useful insight. Taste is what helps you choose between them.

I think there are a few components. Is this question important? Is it tractable — can you actually make progress with the tools and time you have? And if you got an answer, would it change how you think about something, or help you decide what to do next?

And it’s not just choosing a project at the beginning. As you do experiments, you’re constantly making judgments: is this result interesting? Is it a distraction? Should I spend another week understanding this weird thing, or move on? A lot of research is making those decisions under uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response describes research taste as the ability to judge which questions and approaches are promising and to make ongoing research decisions under uncertainty, capturing good high-level decision-making in a project.

r002.rationale: It discusses judging experimental results and whether to continue investigating, but does not identify low-level experimental design as part of research taste.

sol-6.1.text:
By research taste, I mean the ability to choose good problems to work on, and good approaches to those problems. There are lots of questions you could ask, and lots of experiments you could run. The hard part is figuring out which ones are likely to teach you something important.

And I think that involves a few different judgements. Is this question important? Is it tractable? If I got an answer, would it actually change how I think about the problem? And is there a cheap experiment I can do that would help me decide whether to invest more time?

It’s partly an intuition you develop through doing research: making predictions about what will be promising, seeing where you were wrong, and gradually getting better at that.

r001.rationale: Defines research taste as choosing good problems and approaches, and describes it as an intuition developed through research.

r002.rationale: Includes choosing which experiments to run and assessing whether a cheap experiment can guide further investment.
